## Learning objectives {#ch13-01 .balanced .stepwise}

- Prepare and validate a four-table sales model.
- Predict which rows a filter will retain.
- Choose appropriate counts and summaries.
- Design a report whose evidence remains visible.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: frame the chapter as a reporting task. Allow 60-90 seconds. Managers want to ask their next question without requesting another worksheet. We will build that capability on a reconciled model, then test what each interaction actually means. The tutorials use the public Charles River workbook. Misconception to address: a polished page establishes the reliability of its model. Pause and ask: Which control from the Excel chapters should survive the move into Power BI? Transition: introduce the reader and decision.
:::

# Prepare the sales evidence {#ch13-module-2}

::: {.notes}
This module separates loading and preparation from modeling and visual design. Keep the source workbook unchanged and save the report as a separate authoring file.
:::

## The sales manager wants the next question {#ch13-03 .balanced .stepwise}

Where is revenue concentrated?

Which sales carry discounts?

What changes when we select a product group?

::: {.notes}
Purpose: start with decisions and follow-up questions. Allow 60-90 seconds. A static total can answer one question, but the manager may then ask about a segment, region, or month. A report makes those paths available. The evidence still needs a stated period, population, and measure. Read the three questions in turn and ask students to name the fields each requires. Misconception to address: interactivity automatically explains the cause of a result. Pause and ask: Which question needs a grouping field, and which needs a rate? Transition: locate the stages of the work.
:::

## Preparation, model, and report have different jobs {#ch13-04 .balanced .stepwise}

**Power Query:** shape the source tables.

**Semantic model:** relate tables and define calculations.

**Report:** present evidence and guide selections.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: distinguish the three authoring stages. Allow 60-90 seconds. Connect these stages to prior work: repeatable preparation replaces a chain of manual edits, relationships carry filters, and the report exposes selected results. A mistake in one stage can appear as a visual problem in another. Refresh repeats preparation against the source. Misconception to address: dragging a field onto a chart repairs missing or duplicated records. Pause and ask: Where would you correct a date type, and where would you correct a relationship? Transition: separate authoring from distribution.
:::

## Desktop authors; the service distributes {#ch13-05 .balanced .stepwise}

Build and test the report in **Power BI Desktop**.

A report can contain several pages of visuals.

The service supports publishing, sharing, and dashboards.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: clarify the product vocabulary used in the book. Allow 60-90 seconds. The chapter tutorials work in Desktop. A service dashboard is a separate surface of pinned tiles, while a report supports the pages and interactions we are building. A locally saved PBIX is the working artifact for this chapter. Licensing and distribution choices belong to the publishing guidance, not this exercise. Misconception to address: every report page is a service dashboard. Pause and ask: What file will you save after today's tutorial? Transition: prepare the source connection.
:::

## Choose the named Excel Tables {#ch13-06 .balanced .stepwise}

Open **CharlesRiver.xlsx** through Get data.

Select Customer, Item, SalesInvoice, and SalesInvoiceLine.

Use **Transform Data** to inspect the queries.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: start from stable table boundaries. Allow 60-90 seconds. The workbook exposes named Excel Tables as well as worksheet surfaces. Choose the named Tables so the query reads the defined objects. Inspect names, types, required columns, and missing values before loading. The source workbook remains the supplied dataset; preparation belongs in the report queries. Misconception to address: a worksheet preview and a named Table always identify the same range. Pause and ask: How will you recognize the four objects in Navigator? Transition: set the model defaults deliberately.
:::

## Make relationships and dates deliberate {#ch13-07 .balanced .stepwise}

Turn off automatic relationship detection for this model.

Turn off Auto date/time for this file.

Create and inspect each intended relationship.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: avoid hidden modeling assumptions. Allow 60-90 seconds. Follow Tutorial 13.1 for the option locations in the supported Desktop version. These choices keep guessed links and hidden calendars from changing the teaching model. They are deliberate choices for this workflow; students should be able to explain the resulting model rather than simply repeat clicks. Misconception to address: similar column names prove that two columns form a valid key relationship. Pause and ask: What evidence would establish the one side of a relationship? Transition: inspect the full population.
:::

## The preview can hide the promotion population {#ch13-08 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-13/_profile.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: show why profiling scope matters. Allow 60-90 seconds. The first invoice lines precede the promotions. Their profile therefore describes an early slice of history, not the business over the full teaching period. Read the row counts, empty promotion IDs, and distinct discount values together. A missing promotion ID can be expected for a sale without a promotion. Misconception to address: an empty promotion field in the initial preview means the field is useless. Pause and ask: Which conclusion changes when the scope becomes the entire table? Transition: change the profiling scope before cleaning.
:::

## Profile the entire dataset before deciding {#ch13-09 .balanced .stepwise}

Enable column quality, distribution, and profile.

Change the profiling scope to the **entire dataset**.

Interpret errors, empties, and unusual values in context.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: turn the sampling lesson into an action. Allow 60-90 seconds. Use the status control at the bottom of Power Query to change the profiling scope. Inspect the Discount and PromotionID columns again. A preview is useful for shaping a query, but decisions to remove a column or replace missing values need evidence about the population. Microsoft documents the default first-1,000-row scope in its data-profiling guidance. Misconception to address: every blank is an error that should be filled with zero. Pause and ask: What business event would produce a legitimate blank PromotionID? Transition: preserve types and identifiers.
:::

## Types and identifiers carry meaning {#ch13-10 .balanced .stepwise}

Use date types for invoice dates.

Keep keys and descriptive codes as identifiers.

Retain the columns needed to trace a displayed result.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: protect meaning during preparation. Allow 60-90 seconds. The same preparation principles from Chapter 5 apply. A date-looking string is not yet a date, and a numeric customer key is not a quantity. Keep enough document and line identifiers to return from a result to its evidence. A model should make aggregation convenient without discarding traceability. Misconception to address: every numeric column should be added or averaged. Pause and ask: Which columns would you need to trace one unusual sale? Transition: apply the prepared queries.
:::

## Tutorial 13.1: inspect before loading {#ch13-11 .balanced .stepwise}

Confirm the four query names and column types.

Explain the difference between sample and full profiling.

Close & Apply, then save **Charles River Reports.pbix**.

[Open Tutorial 13.1](https://aa.accountinganalyticshub.com/chapters/13-power-bi-essentials/chapter.html#guided-tutorial-13.1-loading-relating-and-reconciling-the-sales-tables)

::: {.notes}
Purpose: pause for preparation and a visible checkpoint. Allow 3-5 minutes. Allow students to complete the public tutorial steps in their own report. Ask them to record what changed in the full-table profile rather than merely report that loading succeeded. Reopen the query steps if a model field has an unexpected type. Save a separate report file beside the source. Misconception to address: a successful load proves the preparation was correct. Pause and ask: Which observed profile difference did you record? Transition: inspect the filter paths.
:::

# Relate and reconcile {#ch13-module-12}

::: {.notes}
A relationship is a path for filters. Students should predict the path before trying it, then reconcile the model to independent controls.
:::

## The model carries filters to invoice lines {#ch13-13 .balanced}

![](/_shared/generated/chapter-13/filter-path.svg){fig-alt="Customer filters SalesInvoice, SalesInvoice filters SalesInvoiceLine, and Item filters SalesInvoiceLine through one-to-many, single-direction relationships." width=95%}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: read the direction of the model. Allow 60-90 seconds. Follow Customer to invoice headers and then to lines. Item reaches the line table directly. Each arrow is a filter direction, not a document workflow or a physical movement of goods. The focused view uses the same keys as the book model, checked against the pinned dataset. Misconception to address: a relationship sends a filter both ways by default. Pause and ask: Can an Item selection travel from the lines back to the invoice headers? Transition: test the key side of each link.
:::

## The one side needs a valid key {#ch13-14 .balanced .stepwise}

Check uniqueness on the one side.

Check that foreign-key values find their parent.

Use a single filter direction from one to many.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: establish the relationship controls. Allow 60-90 seconds. A one-to-many label is a claim about the keys. Check the key population and unmatched values before relying on it. The Charles River model uses explicit relationships because the source does not declare the relationships for Power BI to import automatically. Duplicate labels are not duplicate keys, so test identifiers. Misconception to address: choosing Both is a general solution to an unresponsive visual. Pause and ask: Which test separates duplicate names from duplicate keys? Transition: preserve the event grain.
:::

## A line and an invoice are different counts {#ch13-15 .balanced .stepwise}

**Invoice lines:** count line rows.

**Invoices:** count distinct invoice IDs among those lines.

Choose the count that follows the intended selection.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: distinguish event counts from document counts. Allow 60-90 seconds. Several lines can belong to one invoice. Counting those lines measures line activity; counting unique invoice IDs measures the invoices represented in the current line population. Distinct invoices across product groups need not add to a grand total because one invoice can contain several groups. Misconception to address: a distinct count is additive across every grouping. Pause and ask: Could the same invoice appear in both Furniture and Lighting? Transition: reconcile the unfiltered model.
:::

## Validate the model before designing the report {#ch13-16 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-13/_validation.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: use independent controls before visual formatting. Allow 60-90 seconds. Filter the validation page to fiscal 2026 and compare the displayed line count and revenue with the earlier chapter controls. Count invoices distinctly from the line table. Also inspect the item-group list for an unexpected Blank member. Reconciliation supports the modeled population, while source completeness still requires its own evidence. Misconception to address: matching one revenue total rules out every modeling error. Pause and ask: Why retain both a row count and an amount control? Transition: predict a product selection.
:::

## Predict the selection before clicking {#ch13-17 .balanced .stepwise}

Select **Furniture** in an Item slicer.

The invoice-line amounts should change.

An invoice-header count may remain unchanged.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: make filter direction observable. Allow 60-90 seconds. Trace the Item arrow into the lines and stop there. Under the single-direction model, the selection does not travel backward into SalesInvoice. A distinct count of the invoice key on the lines responds because it is evaluated over retained lines. This static sequence reproduces the reasoning without requiring an embedded live report. Misconception to address: a header count that does not change proves the slicer is broken. Pause and ask: Which table should supply the invoice identifier for this count? Transition: compare the two displayed states.
:::

## The selected state has a different population {#ch13-18 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-13/_selection.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: compare complete static states of an interaction. Allow 60-90 seconds. Read the all-groups state first, then the Furniture state. Both use fiscal 2026, but their retained line populations differ. The invoice count refers to invoices represented among those lines. Ask students to explain the route from the filter field to each result before they reproduce it in Desktop. Misconception to address: the selected revenue is a separate calculation maintained by hand. Pause and ask: Which parts of the filter context stayed the same? Transition: choose aggregation deliberately.
:::

## Do not let a visual choose the business meaning {#ch13-19 .balanced .stepwise}

Set key and year columns to **Don't summarize**.

Check whether the visual is using sum, count, or distinct count.

Name the measure so the reader can interpret it.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: recognize implicit aggregation choices. Allow 60-90 seconds. Dragging a field into a value well creates a summary. Its default is a software choice rather than an accounting definition. A sum of customer IDs is meaningless even though it is computable. Confirm the visual field settings and use readable titles that state the measure and scope. Misconception to address: a field name fully describes the aggregation used in a visual. Pause and ask: What would a label such as Count of SalesInvoiceID actually count? Transition: compare two ways to summarize a rate.
:::

## An average rate can answer the wrong question {#ch13-20 .balanced}

{{< include /_shared/generated/chapter-13/_discount-rate.qmd >}}

::: {.notes}
Purpose: motivate explicit measures without overloading the first model. Allow 60-90 seconds. The unweighted mean treats each line equally. The dollar-weighted rate relates discount dollars to the dollars before discount. Larger discounted lines receive more weight in the latter question. These are different definitions, not rounding differences. Chapter 14 will make the intended ratio an explicit measure. Misconception to address: Average of Discount is automatically the share of revenue discounted. Pause and ask: Which denominator matches a question about discount dollars? Transition: complete the model checkpoint.
:::

## Tutorial 13.2: prove the model {#ch13-21 .balanced .stepwise}

Inspect each one-to-many relationship and its arrow.

Reconcile the Validation page.

Demonstrate the Item filter with a count from the lines.

[Open Tutorial 13.2](https://aa.accountinganalyticshub.com/chapters/13-power-bi-essentials/chapter.html#guided-tutorial-13.2-building-the-sales-and-discounts-page)

::: {.notes}
Purpose: require evidence that the model behaves as intended. Allow 3-5 minutes. Students should show the relationships and the validation page, then explain one selection before they make it. Investigate a Blank item group or changed control total before formatting the report. Keep the saved PBIX as the starting point for the next tutorial. If students start here, use the Companion Files project from the end of Tutorial 13.1; point it at the local CharlesRiver.xlsx, refresh, and save Charles River Reports.pbix before beginning. Misconception to address: a matching screenshot is more important than a reconciled model. Pause and ask: What would you inspect first if the row count increased? Transition: design for the reader's task.
:::

# Design the report for interpretation {#ch13-module-22}

::: {.notes}
Choose a visual because it supports the decision. Make the important scope and comparisons understandable in both interactive use and a static teaching view.
:::

## Match the visual to the question {#ch13-23 .balanced .stepwise}

**Card:** one defined number and its scope.

**Table or matrix:** exact values and comparisons.

**Chart:** patterns across categories or time.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: select evidence displays by task. Allow 60-90 seconds. A manager checking an exact amount needs a different display from one scanning a monthly trend. A chart and a table can complement one another. Position along a common scale generally supports comparisons more clearly than decorative areas or angles; the chapter references the graphical-perception literature. Misconception to address: more visual variety makes a page more informative. Pause and ask: Which display would you choose to verify an exact reconciliation? Transition: make selection behavior visible.
:::

## Filtering and highlighting are different responses {#ch13-24 .balanced .stepwise}

A filter retains the selected population.

A highlight marks a contribution within a wider population.

Use **Edit interactions** to inspect each response.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: separate two visual interaction behaviors. Allow 60-90 seconds. Demonstrate one selection in the working report and identify whether each target visual filters, highlights, or stays unchanged. A partially highlighted bar carries a different denominator from a filtered total. Use a static before-and-after screenshot when recording if the interaction is hard to follow. Misconception to address: every visual on a page responds in exactly the same way. Pause and ask: What total remains visible in a highlighted bar? Transition: expose the meaningful filters.
:::

## A number needs visible context {#ch13-25 .balanced .stepwise}

Show the reporting period.

Show selections that change the meaning of the result.

Provide a clear route back to the default state.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: keep the scope available to the reader. Allow 60-90 seconds. A hidden page or visual filter can change a result while leaving its title unchanged. Use visible slicers, clear labels, or explanatory text for decisions that matter. Test the default opening state and the route to clear selections. Students should be able to explain a copied chart outside the live report. Misconception to address: the reader will inspect every item in the Filters pane. Pause and ask: What information would be lost if this visual were pasted into an email? Transition: evaluate the scale of a chart.
:::

## The axis can exaggerate a small change {#ch13-26 .balanced .stepwise}

Inspect the scale and baseline.

Use a zero baseline for comparisons encoded by bar length.

State a restricted line-chart range clearly.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: evaluate how scale changes perception. Allow 60-90 seconds. A line chart can legitimately use a restricted range to inspect variation, but readers need enough context to judge its size. Bars encode values by length and generally need a zero baseline for that comparison. Have students describe the numerical change before interpreting the apparent steepness of a line. Misconception to address: a dramatic-looking slope proves a dramatic economic change. Pause and ask: What would happen to the visual impression if the scale doubled? Transition: avoid comparisons between unrelated scales.
:::

## Two axes can create a false visual relationship {#ch13-27 .balanced .stepwise}

Identify the unit on each axis.

Do not compare the heights of unrelated measures.

Consider aligned panels with clear labels.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: explain the danger of a dual-axis comparison. Allow 60-90 seconds. Two series can be made to cross or move together by changing one axis range. A common picture does not put revenue dollars and a percentage on a common numerical scale. Separate panels or a carefully defined indexed comparison may communicate the question more honestly. Misconception to address: a crossover means the two business quantities became equal. Pause and ask: What exactly would equality mean when the units differ? Transition: check the starting period.
:::

## An unusual baseline changes the story {#ch13-28 .balanced .stepwise}

Ask why the comparison starts in that period.

Identify startup or incomplete periods.

Compare like periods before describing growth.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: connect coverage to trend interpretation. Allow 60-90 seconds. Charles River's startup month is an unusual base for a growth comparison. The arithmetic can be correct while the implied story is misleading. Keep the baseline visible and test whether the conclusion survives comparison with a representative period. Dates and coverage are analytical assumptions, not just axis labels. Misconception to address: the earliest available period is always the most informative baseline. Pause and ask: What other period would help evaluate the apparent growth? Transition: make the report accessible.
:::

## Make the evidence accessible {#ch13-29 .balanced .stepwise}

Use direct labels and adequate contrast.

Pair color with words, symbols, or line patterns.

Write alternative text that explains the visual's purpose.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: translate accessibility into concrete authoring choices. Allow 60-90 seconds. A reader should not need to distinguish two colors to identify an exception. Direct labels and consistent conventions also help a classroom audience and a recorded lesson. Alternative text should identify the measure, scope, and intended comparison rather than simply repeat that the object is a chart. Reading order and keyboard behavior need inspection in the actual report. Misconception to address: adding a color legend alone makes a visual accessible. Pause and ask: How could a grayscale copy preserve the intended distinction? Transition: complete the report activity.
:::

## Tutorial 13.3: explain one interaction {#ch13-30 .balanced .stepwise}

Build the sales-and-discounts page.

Capture the default state and a selected state.

Explain the population, aggregation, and visual scale.

[Open Tutorial 13.3](https://aa.accountinganalyticshub.com/chapters/13-power-bi-essentials/chapter.html#guided-tutorial-13.3-correcting-three-misleading-charts)

::: {.notes}
Purpose: combine reporting and interpretation in a checkpoint. Allow 3-5 minutes. Ask each student or pair to show the two states and explain what changed without relying on the cursor. Keep the Validation page alongside the presentation page. Review whether a hidden filter, rate average, or axis choice could mislead the manager. Save the report for Chapter 14. If students start here, use the Companion Files project from the end of Tutorial 13.2, reconnect CharlesRiver.xlsx, refresh, and save Charles River Reports.pbix. Misconception to address: a report is finished when the visuals fit on the page. Pause and ask: Which design decision most affects the reader's conclusion? Transition: revisit the learning objectives.
:::

## A trustworthy page rests on a tested model {#ch13-31 .balanced .stepwise}

Preparation describes the whole population.

Relationships and counts follow the intended grain.

The display makes scope and comparisons understandable.

::: {.notes}
Purpose: revisit the chapter's three controls. Allow 60-90 seconds. Return to the manager's questions. Students can now prepare the tables, predict a selection, and explain what each visual summarizes. The remaining limitation is that implicit summaries cannot express every business ratio reliably. The next chapter will define explicit measures and organize a sales star. Misconception to address: visual polish substitutes for population and calculation controls. Pause and ask: Which check would you repeat after changing a relationship? Transition: introduce explicit measures in Chapter 14.
:::
